summary: This informational memo lists requirements for a protocol that carries authentication for network access (PANA). Today the mechanisms for authenticating to a network depend on the access technology, so a single IP-based protocol would work across many link types.

eli5.summary: Each kind of network connection has its own way of checking who you are. This document describes what a single common way of doing it should be able to do.

questions: protocol for carrying authentication for network access
pana requirements for network access authentication
what is an enforcement point in pana
subtitle: What a single, link-independent protocol for logging a device into a network would have to do.

tldr.problem: Ways of authenticating a device to a network depend on the link type: 802.1X works only on IEEE 802 links and PPP only on point-to-point ones. Operators of other networks are left with ad-hoc solutions.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists requirements for a link-layer agnostic protocol that carries existing authentication (such as EAP) between a client and an agent in the access network. It does not design the protocol or any new security mechanism.
tldr.outcome: The requirements define and limit the scope of the PANA working group's protocol work. The RFC is Informational and specifies no standard.

today: RFC 4058 is an Informational requirements memo published in May 2005, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It specifies no protocol itself.

sections.title: The Problem PANA Would Solve
sections.content:
Future IP devices are expected to use many access technologies. Today the mechanisms that give client information to the network for authentication and authorization are tied to the access medium or topology: 802.1X for IEEE 802 links, PPP for point-to-point links.

Appendix A explains the gap. Without a suitable link-layer mechanism, operators use non-standard ad-hoc solutions above the link, add shim layers, or misuse existing protocols. DSL networks that do not use PPP are one example: their operators are left with a web-based login (captive portal) or best-effort service only, and the memo calls the captive portal scheme a non-standard solution with limitations and security flaws.

The goal is a network-layer protocol that works over any link layer that supports IP. IEEE 802.1X and PPP can keep being used in their own domains, but the memo says they do not remove the need for a protocol like PANA.
sections.eli5: A hotel, a library and a cafe each check your ticket differently. This document asks for one ticket check that works everywhere, so nobody has to invent clumsy tricks.

sections.title: The Cast of Characters
sections.content:
The memo defines five terms. The PANA Client (PaC) runs on the host and provides credentials to prove its identity. The PANA Authentication Agent (PAA) sits on the access network side, verifies the credentials and grants network access to the device.

The PaC Identifier (PaCI) is what the client presents, for example a username or an NAI. The Device Identifier (DI) is the handle the network uses to control a client's access; depending on the technology it may contain an IP address, a link-layer address or a switch port number.

An Enforcement Point (EP) is a node where per-packet filters are applied to client traffic. The PAA provides the DI, and optionally cryptographic keys, for building those filters.
sections.eli5: There is a visitor (the client), a guard who checks the visitor's papers (the agent), and a gate that opens only for approved visitors (the enforcement point).

sections.title: Authentication Requirements
sections.content:
PANA MUST enable authentication of clients for network access, and it grants access to the device identified by the DI, not to separate users of the device. It MUST NOT define new security protocols; it is a carrier for existing ones. EAP is named as a candidate payload.

Both sides MUST be able to perform mutual authentication, although the memo notes that clients may not need to authenticate the network when physical security exists, as in dial-up. PANA MUST support periodic and on-demand re-authentication, and either side MUST be able to start both initial authentication and re-authentication. It MUST also be able to run two independent authentications, such as two EAP methods, for one client, because a network access provider and an ISP may both want to authenticate.

Protecting data traffic afterwards is out of scope. EAP keys can feed a separate secure association protocol that creates IPsec security associations, and that protocol MUST be able to enable IPsec-based access control on the EPs. PANA SHOULD allow many identifier types for the PaCI and the DI, and the PAA MUST be able to bind a PaCI to its DI after a successful exchange.

Authorization is limited to plain network access. Carrying accounting data, fine-grained service authorization and access control itself are all outside PANA's scope.
sections.eli5: The wish list says: carry any ID check that already exists, let both sides check each other when needed, and let the check be repeated later. It must not invent a new secret handshake.

sections.title: Network and Deployment Requirements
sections.content:
The PAA does not have to sit on the EP. When they are separate, another protocol must carry the authorization information, including the DI and cryptographic keys, from the PAA to the EPs, and that communication MUST be secure. The working group is to prefer an existing protocol, with COPS, SNMP and Diameter named as candidates.

The PAA and client MUST be exactly one IP hop apart, with no routers between them. Because the client may not know the PAA's address, PANA MUST define a dynamic discovery method. It MUST support clients with multiple interfaces and networks with multiple routers, and MUST NOT assume a secure channel, a connection-oriented link or a point-to-point link. PANA MUST protect against replay attacks and SHOULD have a disconnect indication mechanism, secured against abuse for denial of service.

The client MUST already have an IP address before running PANA, and PANA MUST work with both IPv4 and IPv6. It MUST provide congestion control, for example through delayed initialization and exponential back off, and it MUST resist denial of service such as blind masquerade attacks using IP spoofing.
sections.eli5: The guard has to stand right next to the visitor, must be findable without being told where to stand, and can send the gate its list of approved visitors over a safe line. Nobody should be able to jam the guard's desk with fake visitors.

sections.title: Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
Appendix B groups networks by lower-layer security: physically secured ones such as DSL, ones where the radio link is already encrypted such as cdma2000, and ones with no lower-layer security, where PANA can bootstrap per-packet authentication and integrity protection. It also says PANA suits small deployments such as home and personal area networks, and that authentication can be deferred until a client wants differentiated services.

Five figures show where the PAA can sit relative to the EP and the access router (AR): with the EP only, with the AR only, with both, or separate from both. When they are separate, a different protocol delivers the access control parameters and PANA plays no role in that step.
sections.eli5: The guard can stand at the gate, in the lobby, or in a separate office. The rules for checking papers stay the same wherever the guard stands.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Most of the requirements are security related, and the memo does not specify the protocol itself. Threats are discussed in RFC 4016, and the memo says those threats are already covered by its requirements. It also notes that client identity privacy is outside PANA's scope, though carrying an EAP method that protects identity can provide it.
sections.eli5: This is a plan, not the finished lock. The safety checks are already part of the wish list.
